fuente.nota: Text shortened by paragraphs; the sentences are unchanged.

parrafos: People meet to decide about new laws, and changes to existing ones. This is usually called direct democracy. It is never used except in small countries, or perhaps in towns. Modern populations are usually too large to do this.
The people elect their leaders. These leaders make decisions about laws. This is called representative democracy. Elections are either held after a certain time, or when a leader dies.
Sometimes, people are chosen to make decisions more or less at random. For example, when choosing a jury for a trial. In Europe, trials with a jury are usually used for serious crimes.

The type of government where only one person has most of the power is called a dictatorship. Democracy is the opposite of a dictatorship. Dictatorships often act against freedom of expression so people cannot say bad things about the dictator or replace them for somebody else.

In an election, the people use different ways to choose their leaders. In many countries, the person who gets the most votes wins. But there are many other ways to elect leaders. Very often, the politicians being elected belong to a political party. Instead of choosing a person, people vote for a party. The party with the most votes then picks the leaders. There are multiple ways the party chooses the leader.
Usually, the people being elected need to meet certain conditions: They need to have a certain age or have certain things be able to perform the job.
Not everyone can vote in an election. Suffrage is only given to people who are citizens. Young people are usually excluded, and some other people such as prisoners.
For some elections, a country may make voting compulsory. Someone who does not vote and who does not give a good reason usually has to pay a fine.

In a direct democracy, every adult has the right to vote on individual laws. A modern example of direct democracy is a referendum, which is the name for deciding a law where everyone in the community votes on it. Direct democracies are not usually used to run countries. It is not practical to have everyone voting on everything.

In an indirect, or representative democracy, people choose representatives to make laws for them. These people can be mayors, councilmen, members of Parliament, or other government officials. This is the usual kind of democracy. Large communities like cities and countries use this method, but it may not be needed for a small group.

A term for democracies which are not actually democracies. For example, a constitution of a country may be democratic, but ways are found to interfere with elections. The classic case is Russia, where other candidates that are not in power are not allowed to state their case on any of the state-controlled media. Elections for President are fixed, but the state can claim democratic legitimacy, because in principle other candidates may stand for election. Opposition candidates have no access to the media, and may be harassed in various ways. This is the way all the former parts of the Soviet Union are governed. This does not mean the governments are always bad governments. It does mean that holding "fixed" elections deprives the people of a fair vote. Not surprisingly, these countries have Presidents who are never beaten in an election. They may serve for eight years or longer before retiring. The next leaders are pre-chosen by discussion between the leading families. The elections are often rigged and unfair. The people in power likely stay in power.

Democracy was developed long ago by the Greeks in classical Athens. There, everyone who was a citizen (not slaves, women, foreigners, and children) got together in one area. The assembly would talk about what kinds of laws they wanted and voted on them. The council would suggest the laws. All citizens were allowed in the assembly.

The council were picked by draws (lottery). The participants in the council would change every year, and the number of people in the council was at the most 500. For some offices, the Athenian citizens would pick a leader by writing the name of their favorite candidate on a piece of stone or wood. The person with the most votes became the leader.

In the Middle Ages, there were many systems, although only a few people could join in at this time. The Parliament of England began with Magna Carta, a document which said that the King's power was limited, and protected certain rights of the people. The first elected parliament was De Montfort's Parliament in England in 1265.

However, only a few people could actually join in. Parliament was chosen by only a few percent of the people (in 1780, fewer than 3% of people joined in). The ruler also had the power to call parliaments. After a long time, the power of Parliament began to grow. After the Glorious Revolution in 1688, the English Bill of Rights 1689 made Parliament more powerful. Later, the king or queen became a symbol instead of having real power.
Democratic consolidation means how a new democracy grows up. Once mature, it is unlikely to go back to being a dictatorship without a shock from the outside.

Unconsolidated democracies suffer from elections which are not free and fair. In other words, powerful groups are able to prevent the system working fairly. Some countries are democracies, but then become less so because of the people in power who change the rules to stay in power. This is often gradual.
resumen_es: Explains the forms of democracy (direct, representative, by lot), how elections work and who votes, “pseudo-democracies”, and its origins in Athens and the English Parliament, up to democratic consolidation and backsliding.
nivel_motivo: Although the vocabulary includes some political terms, the sentences are short and very simple (Simple English), so the text is accessible at B1 level.

ideas_clave.idea: Citizens can govern either by voting on laws themselves, which only works in small communities, or by electing leaders, and some decision-makers, such as jurors, are even chosen by lot.
Democracy is the reverse of dictatorship, a regime in which one individual concentrates power and silences criticism.
Electoral systems differ: voters may back individual candidates or parties, and those standing for office must fulfil certain requirements.
The right to vote is restricted to citizens, usually excluding minors and prisoners, and some countries make voting mandatory under penalty of a fine.
Direct democracy survives today mainly through referendums, whereas large communities rely on representatives such as mayors or members of Parliament.
So-called pseudo-democracies keep democratic constitutions but manipulate elections and muzzle the opposition, as the text claims happens in Russia and other post-Soviet states.
Democracy was born in classical Athens, where an assembly of male citizens voted on laws proposed by a council selected by lottery.
In England, Magna Carta and the 1265 parliament started a parliamentary tradition that, although open to very few people, gradually gained power until the monarch became merely symbolic.
Mature democracies rarely revert to dictatorship, while young ones remain vulnerable to unfair elections and to rulers who slowly bend the rules to keep power.

resumen_modelo: The text outlines what democracy is, how it works and how it has evolved. It first distinguishes between direct democracy, in which citizens decide on laws themselves, a model that is only practical in small communities and survives today mainly through referendums, and representative democracy, the usual system, in which voters elect officials to legislate on their behalf. Random selection, as in the choice of juries, is mentioned as a third mechanism. Democracy is presented as the opposite of dictatorship, where a single ruler holds power and suppresses criticism. The article then describes elections: voters may choose individuals or parties, candidates must meet certain requirements, the franchise is limited to adult citizens and, in some countries, abstaining without justification is fined. Furthermore, it warns against pseudo-democracies, which preserve democratic appearances while rigging elections and denying the opposition access to the media. As regards its history, democracy originated in ancient Athens, where an assembly of citizens voted on proposals from a council chosen by lot, and later developed in England, where Parliament, initially elected by a tiny minority, gradually prevailed over the Crown. Finally, the text notes that consolidated democracies seldom collapse, whereas fragile ones may slowly erode when those in power manipulate the rules.

preguntas.enunciado: Say whether the statement is true, false or not stated in the text.
preguntas.pregunta: According to the text, direct democracy is commonly used to govern large modern countries.
preguntas.cita: It is never used except in small countries, or perhaps in towns. Modern populations are usually too large to do this.
preguntas.explicacion: The text says the opposite: direct democracy is only used in small countries or in cities, because modern populations are too large.

preguntas.pregunta: Which example does the text give of people chosen more or less at random to make decisions?
preguntas.cita: Sometimes, people are chosen to make decisions more or less at random. For example, when choosing a jury for a trial.
preguntas.explicacion: The example of random selection is the jury in a trial. Mayors and members of parliament are chosen by voting, and the text does not mention ministers chosen at random.

preguntas.enunciado: Find a word in paragraph 3 that means “a regime in which one person holds almost all the power”.
preguntas.pregunta: Find a word meaning a government in which one person holds most of the power.
preguntas.cita: The type of government where only one person has most of the power is called a dictatorship.
preguntas.explicacion: A “dictatorship”, which the text defines and presents as the opposite of democracy.

preguntas.pregunta: When people vote for a party instead of a person, who picks the leaders?
opciones: The party with the most votes
respuestas: The party with the most votes
preguntas.cita: Instead of choosing a person, people vote for a party. The party with the most votes then picks the leaders.
preguntas.explicacion: According to the text, when people vote for a party, it is the party with the most votes that appoints the leaders. The other options do not appear in the text.

preguntas.enunciado: Say whether the statement is true, false or not stated in the text.
preguntas.pregunta: Prisoners are among the groups that are often excluded from voting.
preguntas.cita: Young people are usually excluded, and some other people such as prisoners.
preguntas.explicacion: The text explicitly mentions prisoners, together with young people, among those who are usually excluded from voting.

preguntas.enunciado: Find a word in paragraph 7 that means “required by law or rules”.
preguntas.cita: For some elections, a country may make voting compulsory.
preguntas.explicacion: “Compulsory” means obligatory: in some countries voting is compulsory and anyone who does not vote without a valid reason pays a fine.

preguntas.enunciado: Say whether the statement is true, false or not stated in the text.
preguntas.pregunta: In countries with compulsory voting, people who do not vote may go to prison.
preguntas.cita: Someone who does not vote and who does not give a good reason usually has to pay a fine.
preguntas.explicacion: The penalty mentioned in the text is a fine, not prison. The detail of the penalty has been changed.

preguntas.pregunta: What is a referendum, according to the text?
opciones: A vote in which everyone in the community decides on a law
An election to choose a new president
A meeting of the council to suggest laws
A vote in Parliament to remove the government
respuestas: A vote in which everyone in the community decides on a law
preguntas.cita: a referendum, which is the name for deciding a law where everyone in the community votes on it
preguntas.explicacion: The text defines a referendum as a vote by the whole community on a law, a modern example of direct democracy. The other options describe other institutions.

preguntas.enunciado: Say whether the statement is true, false or not stated in the text.
preguntas.pregunta: The text states that the governments of pseudo-democracies are always bad governments.
preguntas.cita: This does not mean the governments are always bad governments.
preguntas.explicacion: The text explicitly qualifies that these apparent democracies are not necessarily always bad governments; what it criticises is that they deprive the people of a fair vote.

preguntas.enunciado: Answer in your own words (1–3 sentences).
preguntas.pregunta: Why can a pseudo-democracy still claim democratic legitimacy, according to the text?
respuestas: Because its constitution is formally democratic and, in principle, other candidates may stand for election, even though in practice the opposition has no access to the media, is harassed and elections are fixed.
preguntas.cita: Elections for President are fixed, but the state can claim democratic legitimacy, because in principle other candidates may stand for election.
preguntas.explicacion: The key lies in the difference between theory (anyone can stand) and practice (rigged elections and an opposition without access to the media).

preguntas.enunciado: Say whether the statement is true, false or not stated in the text.
preguntas.pregunta: In classical Athens, women were allowed to take part in the assembly.
preguntas.cita: everyone who was a citizen (not slaves, women, foreigners, and children) got together in one area
preguntas.explicacion: Women, like slaves, foreigners and children, were not citizens and did not take part in the assembly.

preguntas.enunciado: Find a word in paragraph 12 that means “selection by drawing lots” (es: sorteo).
preguntas.pregunta: Find a word meaning a selection made by drawing lots.
preguntas.cita: The council were picked by draws (lottery).
preguntas.explicacion: “Lottery” (and “draws”) indicates that the members of the Athenian council were chosen by lot.

preguntas.pregunta: What proportion of people took part in choosing Parliament in 1780?
preguntas.cita: in 1780, fewer than 3% of people joined in
preguntas.explicacion: The text gives the figure of less than 3 % in 1780 to illustrate how restricted participation was. The other figures do not appear.

preguntas.enunciado: Say whether the statement is true, false or not stated in the text.
preguntas.pregunta: Magna Carta was signed by King John in 1215.
preguntas.explicacion: The text mentions Magna Carta and that it limited the king's power, but gives neither the date nor the king's name.

preguntas.enunciado: Answer in your own words (1–3 sentences).
preguntas.pregunta: How can a democracy become less democratic without a sudden coup, according to the last part of the text?
respuestas: Those in power gradually change the rules so that they can stay in power, and elections stop being free and fair; this is usually a slow process rather than a sudden break.
preguntas.cita: Some countries are democracies, but then become less so because of the people in power who change the rules to stay in power. This is often gradual.
preguntas.explicacion: The text describes democratic backsliding as something gradual, caused by those in power who change the rules in their favour.
